questions.prompt: Match each rung on the five-rung Salesforce analytics career ladder to what actually changes at that level, per Lesson 1.
right: Builds reusable datasets, recipes, and dashboards inside Salesforce's advanced analytics tooling that hundreds of users explore on their own
Answers specific business questions from Salesforce data using native reports, dashboards, SOQL, and presentation tools
Moves Salesforce data into a warehouse such as Snowflake, models it with a tool such as dbt, and version-controls it in Git
Owns the analytics agenda for a function, defines metrics everyone else reuses, and pushes back on requests that would mislead
questions.explain: A Data Analyst answers specific questions with reports, SOQL, and dashboards. A Senior Analyst owns the metric definitions and agenda for a function. A CRM Analytics Developer builds reusable datasets, recipes, and dashboards in Salesforce's advanced analytics tooling for others to explore. An Analytics Engineer moves the data itself into a warehouse, models it, and version-controls it in Git — exactly the four verbs Lesson 1 traces: answer, define and prioritize, build for reuse, engineer the pipeline.

questions.prompt: Select every statement below that correctly describes how to read a job posting, per Lesson 2.
options: Skills repeated in both the summary and the requirements, or tied to the first responsibilities listed, are must-haves worth applying for honestly
A phrase introduced with 'preferred' or 'a plus' is a must-have you should treat as mandatory before applying
A vague phrase like 'data-driven mindset' is a buzzword that tells you little — look for the concrete verbs and tools instead
Titles are company-specific labels, so searching only for postings titled 'Salesforce' anything misses adjacent titles like Sales Operations Analyst or RevOps Analyst that do the same work
questions.explain: Must-haves are the skills repeated in the summary and requirements. 'Preferred' or 'a plus' marks a nice-to-have, not a requirement to treat as mandatory — few candidates match every nice-to-have. Vague phrases like 'data-driven mindset' are buzzwords; look past them to concrete tools and verbs. And because titles vary by company, Lesson 2 explicitly recommends also searching Sales Operations Analyst, RevOps Analyst, Business Systems Analyst, CRM Analyst, and Reporting Analyst.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per the one-page project structure in Lesson 3, after the question, the data, the method, the findings, and the recommendation comes a final section called ________ — where you name sample size, assumptions, and anything you could not verify.
questions.explain: Lesson 3's six-part skeleton ends with Limitations: sample size, assumptions, anything unverified. Naming these builds trust rather than weakening the work, and it is the section career changers are most tempted to skip.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Project 1 defines win rate as Closed Won divided by all closed (won plus lost), by count, over the last ________ completed quarters.
questions.explain: Lesson 4's definitions sheet fixes win rate as Closed Won over all closed deals, by count, across the last four completed quarters — a trailing window chosen specifically so a single slow or lucky quarter doesn't swing the number.

questions.prompt: A rep creates an opportunity manually instead of converting the lead that produced it. Per Lesson 5, which Project 1 question becomes hardest to answer for that deal, and why?
options: Which lead sources convert, because Lead Source is carried onto the opportunity only during conversion, so a manually created opportunity has no reliable source to trace revenue back to
How is each rep pacing against quota, because manually created opportunities are automatically excluded from attainment reports
What is the average sales cycle, because a manually created opportunity has no Created Date field
Which open deals have gone quiet, because manually created opportunities cannot have a Last Activity Date
questions.explain: Lesson 5 is explicit that Lead Source is carried onto the opportunity during conversion — that's what lets revenue be traced back to where it originated. Skip the conversion step and that link never gets made, which breaks the lead-source-conversion question specifically. The opportunity still gets a normal Created Date, Last Activity Date, and owner, so attainment, cycle, and stalled-deal reporting are unaffected.

questions.prompt: Which statement about pipeline coverage is correct, per this course's Project 1 analysis?
options: Coverage is open pipeline divided by the gap to quota, and a healthy-looking ratio can still fall short once you apply the actual win rate.
Coverage is open pipeline divided by the remaining gap to quota, and once that ratio passes 1x, the gap is guaranteed to close no matter what the win rate or deal timing happens to be.
Coverage is total pipeline, open and closed, divided by the annual quota.
Coverage is the trailing win rate divided by the remaining gap to quota.
Coverage only applies to deals that have already closed won, measuring how far past quota the team is.
Coverage is the number of open deals divided by the number of reps on the team.
questions.explain: Lesson 6 defines coverage as open pipeline closing this quarter divided by the remaining gap to quota, then immediately shows why a healthy-looking ratio can mislead: Alder & Vale's 2.5x coverage ($1.35M of pipeline against a $540K gap) looks comfortable, but applying the trailing 35% win rate puts the expected value at only about $473K — short of the $540K gap by roughly $67K.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B states the identical formula and gets the arithmetic right, but adds a claim the lesson directly contradicts: that passing 1x coverage guarantees the gap closes. The whole point of Lesson 6's worked example is that 2.5x coverage, well above 1x, still falls about $67K short once the real win rate is applied — coverage alone never guarantees anything.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: with $1.35M of open pipeline closing this quarter and a trailing win rate of 35%, the expected value of that pipeline is about $473K — short of the $540K gap by roughly $________K.
questions.explain: 35% of $1.35M is about $472,500, rounded to $473K in the lesson. $540K minus $473K is about $67K — the amount by which a seemingly comfortable 2.5x coverage ratio still falls short once the win rate is applied.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about reading rep attainment responsibly, per Lesson 7.
options: Attainment is not the same thing as skill — territory quality, deal timing, and ramp time all affect it
A joined report can show Closed Won and open pipeline as two blocks side by side, grouped by owner, so gap and coverage can be compared per rep
Rep-level dashboard data should be shared as a public leaderboard so reps compete directly against each other
Sharing settings and the dashboard's running user decide who can actually see per-rep numbers, so confirm with the stakeholder who should see them
Tomas having the largest average deal size but the fewest deals means his main problem is that his deals are priced too high
questions.explain: Lesson 7 warns that attainment reflects territory, timing, and ramp, not just skill, and that per-rep visibility depends on the running user and sharing settings, which should be confirmed deliberately. A joined report is exactly how the lesson combines Closed Won and open pipeline by owner. The lesson explicitly frames rep data as coaching material, not a public leaderboard. And Tomas's combination of the largest average deal with the fewest deals points toward too little pipeline volume or early-stage conversion, not pricing.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order Lesson 9 uses to turn Project 1's five reports into a trustworthy dashboard and readout.
items: Build each of the five reports, one per business question, so every widget stays honest
Add each report as a dashboard widget, choosing a deliberate running user
Reconcile every total — confirm the reps' Closed Won sums to the gauge, the stage totals sum to total pipeline, and the lead-source counts sum to total leads
Open the readout with the one-sentence headline finding before explaining method
State risks and limitations, then make one ask tied to a specific decision
questions.explain: Lesson 9's sequence is build the source reports first, turn them into dashboard widgets with a deliberate running user, reconcile every total before anyone sees it, lead the readout with the headline rather than the method, and close with limits and a specific ask — reconciliation happens before presenting, never after.

questions.prompt: A rep insists a $120K deal created two weeks ago will close this quarter. Using Lesson 8's finding that deals over $75K average a 96-day sales cycle, what should this raise for the analyst?
options: Skepticism — a deal that size typically takes about 96 days to close, so one created two weeks ago is unlikely to close this quarter regardless of what close date is entered
No concern — the overall average sales cycle across all deals is about 57 days, which comfortably fits within the quarter
No concern — large deals close faster than small deals in this data, at a 96-day cycle versus 34 days for deals under $25K
Confidence — large deals win more often than smaller ones, at a 30% win rate, so timing is not a real risk factor here
questions.explain: Lesson 8 shows deals over $75K average about 96 days from creation to close, nearly three times the 34-day cycle for deals under $25K. A $120K deal created two weeks ago is far short of that typical cycle, which is exactly the forecasting-insight pattern the lesson applies to flag pipeline that carries timing risk regardless of its stated close date.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Project 2 defines backlog as cases where IsClosed is ________ at the end of the period.
questions.explain: Lesson 10's definitions sheet fixes backlog as cases where IsClosed is false at the end of the period — the first definition locked down before any report gets built.

questions.prompt: Start-of-quarter backlog is 150 open cases. During the quarter, 1,240 cases are opened and 1,180 are closed. Per Lesson 11's backlog equation, what is the end-of-quarter backlog?
options: 210 — backlog at end equals backlog at start, plus opened, minus closed (150 + 1,240 - 1,180)
1,390 — backlog at end equals backlog at start plus every case opened, regardless of how many closed
60 — backlog at end equals cases opened minus cases closed, ignoring the starting backlog
1,240 — backlog at end always equals the number of cases opened in the period
questions.explain: 150 + 1,240 - 1,180 = 210, exactly the figure Lesson 11 has you check against a live report filtered to Closed equals false. The equation needs all three numbers — start, opened, and closed — not just one or two of them.

questions.prompt: Of 1,180 closed cases, 142 breached the resolution target (88% overall compliance), broken down by priority as High 41 of about 177, Medium 78, and Low 23. Select every true statement about this result, per Lesson 12.
options: An 88% headline compliance rate hides that High-priority cases, the most urgent, breach far more often (about 23%) than Low-priority cases (about 6%)
Because High-priority cases are a small share of total volume, their breach rate doesn't meaningfully affect the quality of service
A high escalation rate could mean the team is struggling, or that the process correctly routes hard problems upward — the Escalated checkbox alone doesn't tell you which
If the org has Entitlements and Milestones set up, milestone records are a second possible way to measure SLA compliance besides a row-level breach flag
Correlation between escalation and an SLA breach proves the team is directly at fault for every escalated case
questions.explain: Lesson 12's own point is that the 88% headline hides a much worse 23% breach rate for the most urgent, High-priority cases. It also warns that escalation could reflect struggle or a correctly functioning process, that correlation isn't blame, and that Entitlements/Milestones are a second compliance route if the org has them configured. High-priority cases breaching more often matters precisely because they are urgent, not less because they're a smaller share of volume.

questions.prompt: Match each agent-performance concept from Lesson 13 to what it actually does or shows.
left: Raw average resolution hours by agent
right: Breaks down what share of each agent's closed cases fall into each priority band
A data pitfall where unassigned cases won't appear under any individual agent's name
Can make an agent who handled more Low-priority cases look slowest, even though they aren't actually slower
Computes what an agent's average would be at the team's speed for their own case mix, then compares it to their actual average
questions.explain: A raw average can mislead if an agent's workload skews toward slower case types — that's exactly what the mix matrix exposes, breaking closed cases down by priority per agent. Expected-versus-actual then adjusts for that mix by computing what an agent's time would be at the team's pace given their own mix, and comparing it to what actually happened. Case Owner showing a queue is a separate pitfall: unassigned cases sit under a queue name, not an agent's.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 10, what is the correct way to define 'first response time' if the org has no field that actually tracks it?
options: Say plainly that the org doesn't track it, rather than inventing a value
Estimate it as half of the resolution time
Use the case's Created Date as a stand-in for first response time
Assume it matches the SLA target set for that priority
questions.explain: Lesson 10 is direct about this: 'If the org doesn't track it, say so plainly and don't invent it.' First response time depends on a custom field, an automation, or milestone records that may simply not exist in a given org, and none of the shortcuts in the other options produce a real measurement.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order Lesson 14 uses to turn 'hire someone' from an opinion into a quantified recommendation.
items: Calculate each agent's typical case closures per month (about 98) from the quarter's totals
Compare monthly intake (450) against the team's average monthly closures (393) to find the gap (about 57 cases)
Convert that case gap into a fraction of one agent's monthly capacity (about 0.6 of an agent)
Recommend process fixes first, and frame additional headcount as conditional on intake staying elevated after those changes
questions.explain: Lesson 14 builds the capacity argument in that order: find what one agent typically closes per month, compare monthly intake against the team's average closures to size the gap, convert the gap into a fraction of an agent's capacity, and only then recommend — process changes first, with headcount conditional on intake staying high. Skipping straight to 'hire someone' is exactly the opinion the lesson is correcting.

questions.prompt: The VP of Sales brief for Project 3 asks whether the team is generating enough leads, whether pipeline will reach quota, and whether service problems are putting deals at risk. Per Lesson 15, which of these three requirements is the hardest to turn into a dashboard component, and why?
options: Service risk putting deals at risk — it crosses objects, since Opportunities and Cases only meet indirectly, through the Account
Lead generation — Salesforce cannot report on the Lead object without a separate managed package
Pipeline coverage — there is no way to calculate a remaining gap to quota from Opportunity data
All three are equally simple, since every Project 3 requirement uses the same report type
questions.explain: Lesson 15 calls out the service-risk requirement specifically as 'the hard one' because it crosses objects — Opportunities and Cases don't relate to each other directly, only through a shared Account — which is exactly why Lesson 16 is devoted to combining them. Lead generation and pipeline coverage both reuse native Lead and Opportunity reporting that Project 1 already covered.

questions.prompt: A report joins an Account to its child Opportunities and its child Cases in the same view, and the team notices Opportunity amounts now add up to far more than expected. Per Lesson 16, what is the most likely cause, and what is it called?
options: Fan-out — joining a parent to several children repeats the parent's amount once per matching child row, inflating any sum
A SOQL governor limit was hit, which silently duplicates rows in the result
The report's running user has access to more records than intended
DISTINCT was never applied to the Account Name grouping
questions.explain: Lesson 16 names this directly: when a report joins a parent to several children, the parent's amount repeats for each child, so an Opportunity worth $50K on an Account with three open Cases can appear three times, tripling the sum. The lesson's rule of thumb is that any time totals look too high after adding a related object, suspect fan-out.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 16, select every statement below that correctly describes a native tool for finding accounts with both an open opportunity and an open, high-priority case.
options: Cross filters on an Accounts report return a clean list of at-risk accounts, but they don't total the Opportunity dollars
A custom report type with Accounts as primary can bring in any two unrelated related objects, such as Opportunities and Cases, with no restriction
A joined report can put an Opportunities block and a Cases block side by side, grouped on Account Name, though it carries its own restrictions with charts and dashboards
SOQL with a semi-join, filtering Opportunity by AccountId IN a subquery against Case, can compute an actual dollar total for the at-risk accounts
questions.explain: Lesson 16 is explicit that cross filters give a clean account list without dollar totals, a joined report can show two blocks side by side but with chart/dashboard restrictions, and a SOQL semi-join can compute the actual dollar figure (illustratively, 38 accounts and about $0.4M). Option B is wrong because a custom report type is a chain, not a tree — it generally cannot bring two unrelated siblings like Opportunities and Cases into the same report.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 17, 214 duplicate groups containing 468 leads represent ________ surplus records once each group is reduced to exactly one survivor.
questions.explain: 468 total leads across the duplicate groups, minus the 214 records that are each entitled to survive as the one kept per group, leaves 254 surplus records — the same number Lesson 17 uses afterward to show the conversion rate moving from 15.0% to about 16.1% once they're removed.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a native Salesforce dashboard's running user is correct, per this course?
options: The running user sets what records every viewer sees, regardless of each viewer's own access, so it should be chosen deliberately rather than left to default.
The running user sets what records every viewer of the dashboard sees, but each viewer's own personal record access still additionally limits what they see on top of that.
The running user only controls which components appear on the dashboard, not which records those components show.
Every viewer of a dashboard automatically becomes its own running user, seeing only the records they personally own.
The running user setting only applies to dashboards embedded on a Lightning page, never to a standalone dashboard.
Changing a dashboard's running user requires deleting and rebuilding the dashboard from scratch.
questions.explain: Lesson 18 says a fixed running user 'shows every viewer that person's data,' and warns that 'it also means viewers see records they may not normally access' — the running user's own access governs visibility for everyone, full stop, which is exactly why the course says to choose it deliberately and confirm with the stakeholder who should see per-rep or per-case numbers.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the correct idea that the running user governs visibility, but adds a detail the lesson contradicts: that each viewer's own access still additionally restricts what they see. Lesson 18's own warning is the opposite — a fixed running user 'means viewers see records they may not normally access,' meaning the running user's access applies on its own, without being narrowed back down by each individual viewer's permissions.

questions.prompt: During the Project 3 presentation, the VP says, 'That win rate looks low.' Per Lesson 19, what is the correct response?
options: Define it precisely — explain that the 27% figure is by count, not by amount, and offer to add the by-amount view, rather than defending the number outright
Insist the number is correct and move the conversation forward, since restating a definition mid-presentation undermines credibility
Recalculate the win rate live in the meeting using a different method until it reads higher
Decline to answer, since win rate was not one of the three ranked findings in the presentation
questions.explain: Lesson 19's model response to exactly this pushback is to define the term: '27% is by count, not by amount. Offer to add the by-amount view rather than defending the number.' The lesson's general pattern for pushback is listen, restate the question, answer with data or a definition, and park what you can't answer — never invent a better-looking number on the spot.

questions.prompt: Select every example below of chartjunk that Lesson 20 says should be removed from the executive dashboard.
options: Three-dimensional effects or heavy shadows on bars
One accent color highlighting the thing that matters, with neutral colors used everywhere else
A pie or donut chart with many thin slices
A truncated axis that exaggerates a small change
A component footer stating a KPI's definition and date range
questions.explain: Lesson 20 lists 3D effects and heavy shadows, pie/donut charts with many slices, and truncated axes that exaggerate change as chartjunk to remove. The other two options are the opposite of chartjunk: one accent color for what matters is the lesson's recommended rule, and a definition footer is exactly how the lesson says to carry a KPI's meaning without decoration.

questions.prompt: A reviewer opens your Project 3 dashboard and says they can't tell what the 17 high-priority, five-plus-day-old cases mean without you explaining it out loud. Per Lesson 21's pre-presentation checklist, what is most likely missing?
options: A component title, subtitle, or footer stating the KPI's definition and date range, so the dashboard explains itself without narration
A fourth size band added to the opportunity-amount bucket report
A second running user, so two different people can view the dashboard differently at the same time
A SOQL query embedded directly in the dashboard's description field
questions.explain: Lesson 21's checklist item 1 is 'Definitions: every KPI has a footer stating how it is calculated and the date range,' and Lesson 20's message-title technique says the component itself should carry its meaning. A dashboard that needs live narration to be understood hasn't finished that step yet.

questions.prompt: A dashboard's total doesn't match its source report's total. Per Lesson 22's model answer, what should you check, and in what order?
options: The dashboard's running user, then its filters, then whether the component's source report filters differ from the report you compared it to, then when the dashboard last refreshed
Only whether the dashboard was refreshed recently — nothing else commonly causes this kind of mismatch
Whether the report type is custom or standard, since a custom report type can never match a dashboard total
The org's governor limits, since a dashboard silently drops rows once a query exceeds its row limit
questions.explain: Lesson 22's model answer lists these causes in order: 'the dashboard's running user (which controls what records it sees), dashboard filters, differences between the component's source report filters and the report you compared, and when the dashboard was last refreshed.' Naming them in that order is what the lesson says shows an interviewer you've actually debugged this before.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 23's four-part project story, the four parts are problem, approach, result, and what you'd ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 23's four-part structure ends with 'what I'd change: one honest improvement' — admitting one real flaw, like a hard-coded quota, rather than presenting the project as flawless.

questions.prompt: Match each interview situation to which project Lesson 23 says to lead with.
left: A general analyst role with no strong signal either way
right: Lead with whichever project best fits the specific job description, keeping one-sentence summaries of all three ready
Lead with Project 3, Executive CRM Analytics
questions.explain: Lesson 23 ties Project 1 to sales operations and conversion work, Project 3 to executive-facing, independence-and-communication roles, and Project 2 to case volume, SLA, and agent-performance thinking. Absent a strong signal from the posting, the lesson says to pick whichever fits the actual job description and keep all three summaries ready.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about anchoring and responding to a job offer, per Lesson 24.
options: If you have to state a number first, give a range whose bottom you would happily accept, based on your own research
It's acceptable to mention a competing offer that doesn't actually exist if it strengthens your negotiating position
A reasonable sequence on receiving an offer is: thank them, ask for a day or two, compare it to your researched range and total package, then make one clear counter with a reason
Negotiating base pay and other items, such as a signing bonus or start date, one at a time rather than together, generally produces a better outcome
Letting the employer share their range first, when possible, is one way to avoid anchoring yourself too low
questions.explain: Lesson 24 explicitly instructs never to invent a competing offer, and to negotiate the whole package together rather than one item at a time — the opposite of options B and D. It does recommend anchoring with a range whose bottom you'd accept, letting the employer share their range first when possible, and responding to an offer with thanks, time to review, a comparison to your researched range, and one clear counter with a reason.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 25, why does this path point toward analytics engineering as a next step, rather than treating this course as a finish line?
options: Problems like blending leads, opportunities, and cases, cleaning data at scale, and keeping a quota value current are data-modeling problems that an analytics engineer solves once, upstream, so every downstream dashboard stays consistent
Native Salesforce reporting has no real limitations, so analytics engineering is purely a matter of chasing a better title
The CRM Analytics Developer and Analytics Engineer roles don't use any SQL or data skills already covered earlier in this path
The Advanced stage replaces Salesforce entirely with a different CRM platform
questions.explain: Lesson 25 draws the line directly from Project 3's pain points — blending objects, cleaning data, maintaining a quota value — to analytics engineering: 'an analytics engineer solves them once, upstream, so every dashboard downstream is consistent.' The Advanced stage builds on Salesforce and SQL skills already in hand; it doesn't replace them or ignore them.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a strong scenario-question answer in the order Lesson 22 recommends.
items: Restate the question in your own words
Add a concrete example from your own portfolio
Note a limit or assumption you are making
questions.explain: Lesson 22 states the reliable structure plainly: 'restate the question, describe your approach in order, add a concrete example from your portfolio, and note a limit or assumption.' Following that order every time keeps an answer from rambling or skipping the honesty step at the end.
